title: Dashboards: operations, evals, delivery and spend

story: It is 10 September. You post a screenshot of the new spend panel in the team channel: Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, has spent $1,400 on Claude this month. Within a minute there are two replies. One says "that is a lot". The other says "that seems fine for three weeks of pilot work". Both are guessing, and so are you.

Two weeks later the delivery panel shows merged PRs up from 20 to 30 a week for the frontend team, and someone wants to share it with the whole company. Nobody notices that in the same weeks, five of those PRs needed a fix within days. A single number on a dashboard invites a story, and the story depends on who is looking.
hook.question: How do we build dashboards where a number cannot be read the wrong way?

p: Is $1,400 a lot? It depends on two things the panel did not show: the month's budget, and how far into the month we are. Say Nova's budget is $3,000 a month. If spending were perfectly even, by 10 September, day 10 of 30, Nova would have spent 3,000 × 10 / 30 = $1,000. That straight line from zero on the 1st to the budget on the last day is the line to judge the number against. $1,400 is 40% above it. Now the number means something: at this pace Nova ends the month at about $4,200.

Burn rate is the name for this: how fast a budget is being used, compared with the even pace. Our spend alert compares every scope (people as one scope, and each agent) with its line, every hour, and warns when month-to-date spend is more than 25% above it for six hours in a row. The 25% margin is there because the first days of a month are noisy: one busy Monday can put any scope ahead of an even line. The six hours keep one bad hour from waking anyone.

Read the description line of the rule twice: an alert, never a stop. Nothing pauses an agent when it fires. The alert goes to #ai-agents-alerts, our Slack channel for platform alerts, with the teams or agents that grew most since last week, and people decide.

code.file: alert_rules/ai-spend.yml (one rule; vmalert, the program that checks alert rules, evaluates it)
code.text:
- name: ai-spend
  interval: 1h
  rules:
    - alert: AISpendAheadOfBudget
      expr: |-
        sum by (scope) (last_over_time(ai_spend_mtd_usd[1d]))
          > 1.25 * sum by (scope) (last_over_time(ai_spend_budget_usd[1d]))
          * day_of_month() / days_in_month()
      for: 6h
      labels:
        severity: warning
        service.name: ai-agents
      annotations:
        summary: "[AI spend «{{ $labels.scope }}»] month-to-date is more than 25% ahead of budget"
        description: "An alert, never a stop. The AI spend dashboard shows which teams or agents drive it."

notes.text: The rule runs once an hour. The month-to-date numbers come from the nightly job, once a day.
last_over_time(...[1d]) takes the newest value of the last day. Without it, a query only looks back about five minutes, so a number pushed once a night is invisible to an hourly rule.
1.25 × the even line: the budget times the share of the month that has passed.
The condition must stay true for six hours before the alert fires.

p: The same idea fixes the delivery screenshot. Merged PRs per week is throughput, and throughput alone rewards the wrong thing: it goes up when people split work into smaller PRs, and it goes up when they ship faster than they check. The number that keeps it honest is change failure, the share of merged PRs that needed a revert, a hotfix or a Bug fix within 14 days. So the delivery dashboard never has a panel with merged PRs alone. They share one panel with change failure, on a second axis, so nobody can screenshot one without the other.

In the lab data, the frontend team goes from 20 to 30 merged PRs a week. On the same panel, change failure goes from 5% to almost 17%. That is not "50% more output"; it is a team, or an agent, shipping faster than it can check, and the dashboard says so in one picture. Each delivery panel also draws the baseline from the nightly job, the 12 weeks before October, as a flat reference line, and shows how many PRs each median is based on, because weekly numbers for about 25 engineers jump around.

code.text:
{ "title": "Merged PRs next to change failure", "type": "timeseries",
  "targets": [
    { "refId": "A", "legendFormat": "merged PRs",
      "expr": "sum(delivery_merged_prs{team=~\"$team\"})" },
    { "refId": "B", "legendFormat": "change failure %",
      "expr": "100 * sum(delivery_failed_changes{team=~\"$team\"}) / sum(delivery_merged_prs{team=~\"$team\"})" } ],
  "fieldConfig": { "defaults": {}, "overrides": [
    { "matcher": { "id": "byName", "options": "change failure %" },
      "properties": [ { "id": "custom.axisPlacement", "value": "right" }, { "id": "unit", "value": "percent" } ] } ] } }

notes.text: $team is the dashboard's team variable. There is no person variable on any of our dashboards.
Change failure as a percentage, computed from the same two series the job writes.
An override changes one series only: the percentage gets its own axis on the right, so a small number is not flattened next to a count.

read.h: The partner on the other two screens
p: The operations dashboard is the screen we open when something feels off. It shows cost and tokens per agent, read from the LLM gateway, the service every model call goes through. Cost alone says that something changed, not why, so its partner is the cache-read share: the part of all input tokens that the prompt cache served. Claude can reuse the start of a prompt it has already seen at a much lower price, as long as that start stays exactly the same. When the share falls under 70% the panel turns red, because something now changes the start of the prompt on every turn: a switched model, a tool list that changes, or a timestamp near the top. Cost goes up for a reason you can fix.

The eval scoreboard shows, for each eval suite (a fixed set of test cases that scores an agent), the pass rate of every agent version, model and effort level. Its partner is the spread: every case runs three times, and the pass rate moves a little between rounds. The panel draws the pass rate with a second line for its low edge, the pass rate minus the spread. A new prompt that moves the pass rate from 78% to 80% while the spread is 6 points has not changed anything you can trust. Next to each pass rate sit cost per case and median turns (how many model calls the agent needed for a case), so a right answer reached the long and expensive way still shows.

code.file: the cache-read share, per agent (operations panel and a second alert)

notes.text: Tokens the cache served over the last six hours, per agent, from the gateway's counter.
Divided by all input tokens: new input, cache reads and cache writes. Healthy is 80% or more.

deeper.h: Go deeper: where the dashboards live and what they never show
p: All four dashboards are JSON files in the infrastructure repo, in the AI-Agents folder of the Grafana module. A small helper container next to Grafana, a sidecar, loads every file in that folder, so a new panel is a pull request and a bad edit is a revert. Panels about events, such as API errors and rejected tool calls, read VictoriaLogs with LogsQL instead of VictoriaMetrics with PromQL; the lesson about Grafana dashboards and alerts covers both languages.

No dashboard has a person dimension. People's own Claude Code spend appears only by team; each person can see their own spend in Claude Code's /usage command and nowhere else. Before the delivery dashboard is shared, someone walks a leader through it, because a dashboard that can be misread is worse than none.

lab.title: Put every number next to its line
lab.goal: Store a month's spend and four weeks of delivery numbers, then write the queries that judge each number against its line: the budget pace and change failure.

guess.q: On 10 September (day 10 of 30), month-to-date spend is people $2,150 of $6,000, Nova $1,400 of $3,000, and the CI fixer $150 of $600. Which scopes does the burn-rate alert (more than 25% above the even line) warn about?

options.text: People and Nova, because both will end the month over budget at this pace.
options.why: People will end slightly over ($6,450 against $6,000), but that is only 7.5% ahead of the line. The 25% margin keeps early-month noise quiet.

options.text: Only Nova: its line is $1,000, and $1,400 is 40% above it.
options.why: 1.25 × $1,000 = $1,250, and $1,400 is above that. People's line is $2,000 (limit $2,500) and the CI fixer's is $200.

options.text: None of them, because no scope has spent its whole budget yet.
options.why: That would be an alert that only fires when it is too late to act. The point of the line is to warn on day 10, not on day 31.

follow.say: Make a folder and write two small files of Prometheus text: one month-to-date spend and budget per scope, stamped 10 September, and four weeks of the frontend team's merged and failed PRs.

cat > spend.txt <<'EOF'

ai_spend_mtd_usd{scope="nova"} 1400 1788998400000
ai_spend_mtd_usd{scope="cifix"} 150 1788998400000

ai_spend_budget_usd{scope="nova"} 3000 1788998400000
ai_spend_budget_usd{scope="cifix"} 600 1788998400000
EOF
cat > delivery.txt <<'EOF'
delivery_merged_prs{team="frontend"} 20 1788739200000
delivery_merged_prs{team="frontend"} 22 1789344000000
delivery_merged_prs{team="frontend"} 26 1789948800000
delivery_merged_prs{team="frontend"} 30 1790553600000
delivery_failed_changes{team="frontend"} 1 1788739200000

follow.say: Start VictoriaMetrics with a long retention period, because these points are in the past, and push both files.
follow.do:
docker run -d --name vm-g1-3 -p 8428:8428 victoriametrics/victoria-metrics:v1.154.0 -retentionPeriod=100y && sleep 3
cat spend.txt delivery.txt | curl -s -w '%{http_code}\n' --data-binary @- localhost:8428/api/v1/import/prometheus

follow.say: Define a small helper that asks the database a question as of 10 September, then look at the number everyone screenshots: spend so far.
follow.do:
q() { curl -s localhost:8428/api/v1/query --data-urlencode "query=$1" --data-urlencode 'time=2026-09-10T00:00:00Z' | jq -c '[.data.result[] | [.metric.scope, .value[1]]]'; }
sleep 5 && q 'ai_spend_mtd_usd'

follow.say: Now draw each scope's line: the budget times the share of the month that has passed. day_of_month() and days_in_month() are built into the query language.
Ask the alert's question: which scopes are more than 25% above their line? Each row that comes back would be one alert.
follow.do: q 'sum by (scope) (ai_spend_mtd_usd) > 1.25 * sum by (scope) (ai_spend_budget_usd) * day_of_month() / days_in_month()'

follow.say: Switch to delivery. Define a helper for a range of weeks, then look at merged PRs alone, the way the screenshot showed them.
follow.do:
r() { curl -s localhost:8428/api/v1/query_range --data-urlencode "query=$1" --data-urlencode 'start=2026-09-07T00:00:00Z' --data-urlencode 'end=2026-09-28T00:00:00Z' --data-urlencode 'step=7d' | jq -r '.data.result[] | (.values | map((.[0]|todate[5:10]) + " " + .[1]) | join("  "))'; }
r 'sum(delivery_merged_prs{team="frontend"})'

follow.say: Now its partner: change failure in percent, computed from the same two series. Read both lines together.

lab.build: Write the forecast every spend panel should show next to the month-to-date number: where each scope ends the month at today's pace (spend so far, divided by the day of the month, times the days in the month). Run it with q, compare each result with the budget in spend.txt, and write one sentence for each scope: will it end over budget, and does the alert warn about it? Explain the one scope where the two answers differ.
checks: q 'ai_spend_mtd_usd' shows three scopes, and the even line shows cifix 200, nova 1000 and people 2000.
The alert query returns exactly one row: nova, 1400.
Merged PRs rise from 20 to 30 while change failure rises from 5% to 16.7%.
Your forecast shows cifix 450, nova 4200 and people 6450, and you can say why people ends over budget but does not alert.
After the Fix it step, the alert query asked at 06:00 returns nova again.

solution.text:
q 'sum by (scope) (ai_spend_mtd_usd) / day_of_month() * days_in_month()'
# [["cifix","450"],["nova","4200"],["people","6450"]]
# people ends about 7.5% over its $6,000, which is under the 25% margin, so no alert.
# nova ends 40% over its $3,000, and it alerts.

lab.fix: The spend rule passed review, but it has never fired, even in a week when Nova was 40% ahead. Ask the same alert question at 06:00 instead of midnight: curl -s localhost:8428/api/v1/query --data-urlencode 'query=sum by (scope) (ai_spend_mtd_usd) > 1.25 * sum by (scope) (ai_spend_budget_usd) * day_of_month() / days_in_month()' --data-urlencode 'time=2026-09-10T06:00:00Z' | jq -c '.data.result' and see that it prints []. The nightly job pushes one point a day, and a plain query only looks back about five minutes. Repair the expression so an hourly rule always sees the newest value of the last day, and run it at 06:00 again.
explain: Why is "Nova spent $1,400 this month" not enough to say whether that is good or bad?
Why does the alert allow 25% above the line instead of warning at the first dollar above it?
Why do merged PRs and change failure always share one panel?
lab.done: The alert query names only Nova, also when asked at 06:00, you can explain the forecast for every scope, and you removed the database with docker rm -f vm-g1-3.

check.q: On day 15 of a 30-day month, the CI fixer has spent $280 of its $600 budget. Does the burn-rate alert warn?

options.text: Yes, because it will run out before the month ends
options.why: At this pace it ends at $560, under its budget.

options.text: No: its line is $300, and $280 is below it
options.why: Half the month has passed, so the even line is half the budget, $300. The alert needs more than 1.25 × $300 = $375.

options.text: Yes, because $280 is close to half the budget
options.why: Being near the line is exactly where it should be. The alert is about being far above it.

check.q: After an update to the agent, the frontend team's merged PRs are up 50% in a month. What must the same panel show before anyone shares it?

options.text: Change failure for the same weeks
options.why: More merged PRs with many more failed ones is not progress. Throughput never appears without the number that keeps it honest.

options.text: The merged PRs of each engineer, to see who drove it
options.why: No dashboard has a person dimension. The question is whether the team's delivery got better, not who did it.

options.text: Nothing else; a 50% rise is clear enough
options.why: Throughput rises when PRs get smaller or checks get skipped. Alone, it rewards the wrong thing.

check.q: A prompt change moves an eval suite's pass rate from 78% to 80%. The spread between the three runs is 6 points. What do you conclude?

options.text: The change improved quality by 2 points
options.why: Two points is smaller than the normal variation between runs, so it could be luck.

options.text: The change made things worse, because the spread is large
options.why: A large spread does not mean worse. It means small moves cannot be trusted either way.

options.text: Nothing yet: the move is inside the spread, so it is not a real change
options.why: A change only counts when it moves outside the spread: above the pass rate plus the spread, or below the low edge, the pass rate minus the spread.

p: The four dashboards are JSON files in infrastructure's modules/grafana/dashboards/AI-Agents/: ai-agents-operations.json (cost, tokens and cache-read share per agent from the gateway series, API errors and rejected tool calls from Claude Code events in VictoriaLogs), ai-spend.json (people's spend by team from claude_code_cost_usage_USD_total, agent spend, cost per ticket and per merged agent PR), ai-evals.json (one repeated row per suite with the low edge, cost per case and median turns, and a data link to each run's JSON in S3) and delivery-impact.json (team variable only, baseline lines, counts next to medians, 12-week default range).

The alert rules live in the victoria-metrics unit under alerting/templates/alert_rules/ai-spend.yml: AISpendAheadOfBudget on ai_spend_mtd_usd and ai_spend_budget_usd, which the nightly job writes per scope from spend-limits.yaml, and AICacheReadShareLow per agent under 70% for 2 hours. Both route to #ai-agents-alerts and mention Sean and Nir. The rule as planned reads the daily series without last_over_time, which an hourly rule cannot see; the lesson's version adds it.

tickets.why: The operations dashboard: cost and tokens per agent, cache-read share, errors and rejected tools.
The spend view, the burn-rate alert and the cache-read alert.
The eval scoreboard: pass rate with its low edge, cost per case and median turns.
The delivery-impact dashboard: team level, baseline lines, throughput next to change failure.

words.plain: How fast a budget is being used, compared with spending it evenly over the month.
Everything spent from the 1st of the month until now.
The share of merged PRs that needed a revert, a hotfix or a Bug fix within 14 days.
The part of all input tokens that the prompt cache served. Under 70% means something keeps changing the start of the prompt.
How much a pass rate moves between repeated runs of the same eval. Changes smaller than it are noise.

review.q: Write the burn-rate condition in words, with both numbers that make it calm.
review.a: Month-to-date spend above 1.25 × budget × (day of month ÷ days in month), true for six hours: the 25% margin ignores early-month noise and the six hours ignore one bad hour.

review.q: Name the partner of each number: merged PRs, agent cost, an eval pass rate.
review.a: Change failure; the cache-read share; the spread (low edge), with cost per case and median turns.

review.q: Why does an hourly rule over a nightly series need last_over_time?
review.a: A plain query only looks back a few minutes, so a point written once a night is invisible most of the day; last_over_time(x[1d]) returns the newest value of the last day.

remember: Never show a number alone: put spend next to its budget line, throughput next to change failure, cost next to cache share, and a pass rate next to its spread.
